chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Ibn Muskan, from Ibn Abi Yafur, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a man: Does anything that passes in front of him cut off his prayer? He (peace be upon him) said: Nothing cuts off the prayer of the believer, but ward off (the passerby) as much as you can.

And in a narration of Ibn Muskan from Abu Baseer from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) who said: Nothing cuts off the prayer, neither a dog, nor a donkey, nor a woman, but cover yourself with something. So if there is in front of you a measurement of a cubit raised from the ground, then you have covered yourself.

Al-Kulayni and Al-Fazl said regarding this: You should cover yourself with something and place in front of you what you use to protect yourself from the passerby. If you do not do so, there is no harm in it, because the one for whom the pray-er is praying is closer to him than the one who passes in front of him, but that is the etiquette of the prayer and its reverence.
ai.seo_question: Does something passing in front of a person invalidate their prayer in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith clarifies the distinction between the validity (sahha) and perfection (kamal) of prayer, asserting that while a passerby does not invalidate the prayer, ignoring the sutrah neglects the etiquette (adab) and reverence (tawqir) of the prayer. The commentary by Al-Kulayni and Al-Fadl underscores that the Imam’s intercession is closer to the worshiper than the passerby, making the barrier a means of focusing devotion rather than a strict condition for validity. This reflects the Shia juristic principle of distinguishing between obligatory precautions and recommended adornments of worship.
